concepts.label: The History of Print
concepts.cardText: It is difficult for us to imagine a world without printed matter. Print is all around us in books, journals, newspapers, prints of paintings and everyday things like circulars, calendars and posters. We take this world of print for granted and often forget that there was a time before print, and that print itself has a history which has shaped our contemporary world. The chapter looks at the development of print from its beginnings in East Asia to its expansion in Europe and in India, and at how social lives and cultures changed with the coming of print.

concepts.label: Print in China
concepts.cardText: The earliest print technology was developed in China, Japan and Korea as a system of hand printing. From AD 594 onwards books in China were printed by rubbing paper, also invented there, against the inked surface of woodblocks. Because both sides of the thin, porous sheet could not be printed, the traditional Chinese accordion book was folded and stitched at the side. The imperial state was for a long time the major producer of printed material; a huge bureaucracy recruited through civil service examinations, and textbooks for the examinations were printed in vast numbers under imperial sponsorship, increasing the volume of print as candidates grew after the sixteenth century. By the seventeenth century, as urban culture bloomed, print was no longer used just by scholar-officials: merchants collected trade information, reading became a leisure activity, and rich women read and published poetry and plays. Western printing techniques and mechanical presses were imported in the late nineteenth century, and Shanghai became the hub of the new print culture.

concepts.label: Print in Japan
concepts.cardText: Buddhist missionaries from China introduced hand-printing technology into Japan around AD 768-770. The oldest Chinese book, printed in AD 868, is the Buddhist Diamond Sutra, containing six sheets of text and woodcut illustrations. In medieval Japan poets and prose writers were regularly published and books were cheap and abundant. In the late eighteenth century, in the flourishing urban circles of Edo (later Tokyo), illustrated collections of paintings depicted an elegant urban culture of artists, courtesans and teahouse gatherings, and libraries and bookstores were packed with hand-printed books on subjects such as women, musical instruments, cooking and etiquette. Kitagawa Utamaro, born in Edo in 1753, was widely known for the art form ukiyo, pictures of the floating world, depicting ordinary urban experience.

concepts.label: Print Comes to Europe: Marco Polo and the Need for a New Technology
concepts.cardText: In the eleventh century Chinese paper reached Europe along the silk route, making manuscripts carefully written by scribes possible. In 1295 Marco Polo returned to Italy from China and brought back the knowledge of woodblock printing; Italians began producing books with woodblocks and the technology spread through Europe. Luxury editions were still handwritten on expensive vellum for aristocrats and rich monastic libraries, which scoffed at printed books as cheap vulgarities, while merchants and students bought cheaper printed copies. As demand rose, booksellers exported books and employed scribes, often more than 50 for one bookseller. But handwritten manuscripts could not satisfy the demand: copying was expensive, laborious and time-consuming, and manuscripts were fragile, awkward to handle and hard to carry, so circulation remained limited. By the early fifteenth century woodblocks printed textiles, playing cards and religious pictures with simple texts, but there was a great need for quicker and cheaper reproduction, met when Johann Gutenberg developed the first-known printing press at Strasbourg in the 1430s.

concepts.label: Gutenberg and the Printing Press
concepts.cardText: Gutenberg was the son of a merchant who grew up on a large agricultural estate and had seen wine and olive presses from childhood. He learnt to polish stones, became a master goldsmith and acquired expertise in making lead moulds for trinkets. Drawing on this knowledge he adapted existing technology: the olive press provided the model for the printing press, and moulds were used to cast metal types for the letters of the alphabet. By 1448 he had perfected the system. The first book he printed was the Bible, about 180 copies in three years, which was fast production by the standards of the time. He developed metal types for each of the 26 characters of the Roman alphabet and a way of moving them to compose different words, the movable type printing machine, which remained the basic print technology for the next 300 years; the press could print 250 sheets on one side per hour. The new technology did not entirely displace book production by hand: early printed books resembled manuscripts, with illuminated borders and painted illustrations. Between 1450 and 1550 presses were set up in most European countries, and the second half of the fifteenth century saw 20 million printed copies, rising to about 200 million in the sixteenth century, so that the shift from hand printing to mechanical printing led to the print revolution.

topics.title: The print revolution and its impact

concepts.label: The Print Revolution and a New Reading Public
concepts.cardText: The print revolution was not just a new way of producing books; it transformed people's lives, changing their relationship to information, knowledge, institutions and authorities. With the printing press a new reading public emerged. Printing reduced the cost of books, the time and labour needed to produce each book came down, and multiple copies could be produced with greater ease. Earlier reading was restricted to the elites, and common people lived in a world of oral culture, hearing sacred texts read, ballads recited and folk tales narrated; knowledge was transferred orally. Now a reading public came into being alongside the hearing public. But literacy rates in most European countries were very low till the twentieth century, so printers published popular ballads and folk tales, profusely illustrated, which were sung and recited at gatherings in villages and taverns. Oral culture thus entered print and printed material was orally transmitted, blurring the line between oral and reading cultures.

concepts.label: Religious Debates and the Fear of Print
concepts.cardText: Print created the possibility of wide circulation of ideas and introduced a new world of debate and discussion; even those who disagreed with established authorities could print and circulate their ideas to persuade people to think differently. Not everyone welcomed the printed book. It was feared that if there was no control over what was printed and read, rebellious and irreligious thoughts might spread and the authority of valuable literature would be destroyed. In 1517 Martin Luther wrote the Ninety Five Theses criticising practices of the Roman Catholic Church; a printed copy was posted on a church door in Wittenberg and challenged the Church to debate. His writings were reproduced in vast numbers and widely read, leading to a division within the Church and the beginning of the Protestant Reformation. Luther's translation of the New Testament sold 5,000 copies within a few weeks, and he said printing is the ultimate gift of God and the greatest one.

concepts.label: The Reading Mania
concepts.cardText: Through the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries literacy rates went up in most of Europe. Churches of different denominations set up schools in villages, carrying literacy to peasants and artisans, and by the end of the eighteenth century in some parts of Europe literacy rates were as high as 60 to 80 per cent. As literacy and schools spread there was a virtual reading mania, and printers produced books in ever-increasing numbers. Booksellers employed pedlars who roamed villages carrying little books; there were almanacs, ballads and folktales. In England penny chapbooks carried by chapmen were sold for a penny so that even the poor could buy them, and in France the Biliotheque Bleue were low-priced small books in cheap blue covers. The periodical press developed from the early eighteenth century, combining current affairs with entertainment. The ideas of scientists and philosophers became accessible to common people: Isaac Newton's discoveries reached a wider circle, and the writings of Thomas Paine, Voltaire and Rousseau were widely printed, bringing ideas about science, reason and rationality into popular literature.

concepts.label: 'Tremble, Therefore, Tyrants of the World!'
concepts.cardText: By the mid-eighteenth century there was a common conviction that books were a means of spreading progress and enlightenment. Many believed that books could change the world, liberate society from despotism and tyranny, and herald a time when reason and intellect would rule. In his novels the heroes are transformed by acts of reading, and convinced of the power of print to bring enlightenment and destroy the basis of despotism, he proclaimed: Tremble, therefore, tyrants of the world! Tremble before the virtual writer!

concepts.label: Print Culture and the French Revolution
concepts.cardText: Many historians have argued that print culture created the conditions in which the French Revolution occurred. Three arguments are put forward. First, print popularised the ideas of Enlightenment thinkers, whose writings critically commented on tradition, superstition and despotism, argued for the rule of reason rather than custom, and attacked the sacred authority of the Church and the despotic power of the state; the writings of Voltaire and Rousseau were widely read. Second, print created a new culture of dialogue and debate, in which all values, norms and institutions were re-evaluated by a public aware of the power of reason, and new ideas of social revolution came into being. Third, by the 1780s an outpouring of literature mocked royalty and criticised their morality; cartoons suggested that the monarchy was absorbed only in sensual pleasures while the common people suffered, and this underground literature led to hostile sentiments against the monarchy. But people did not read only one kind of literature; they were also exposed to monarchical and Church propaganda, accepted some ideas and rejected others, so print did not directly shape their minds but opened up the possibility of thinking differently.

concepts.label: Children, Women and Workers as Readers
concepts.cardText: The nineteenth century saw vast leaps in mass literacy in Europe, bringing in large numbers of new readers among children, women and workers. As primary education became compulsory from the late nineteenth century, children became an important category of readers and the production of school textbooks became critical for publishers. A children's press was set up in France in 1857. The Grimm Brothers compiled folk tales from peasants and edited them before publishing in 1812, leaving out anything unsuitable for children or vulgar to the elites, so print recorded old tales but also changed them. Women became important as readers and writers: penny magazines and manuals on behaviour and housekeeping were meant for them, and novelists such as Jane Austen, the Bronte sisters and George Eliot defined a new type of woman with will, strength of personality and the power to think. Lending libraries in England educated white-collar workers, artisans and lower-middle-class people, and after the working day was shortened from the mid-nineteenth century workers had time for self-improvement and wrote political tracts and autobiographies.

concepts.label: Further Innovations in Printing Technology
concepts.cardText: By the late eighteenth century the press came to be made out of metal. By the mid-nineteenth century Richard M. Hoe of New York had perfected the power-driven cylindrical press, capable of printing 8,000 sheets per hour and particularly useful for printing newspapers. In the late nineteenth century the offset press was developed, which could print up to six colours at a time, and from the turn of the twentieth century electrically operated presses accelerated printing. Printers and publishers also developed new strategies to sell their products: nineteenth-century periodicals serialised important novels, which gave birth to a particular way of writing novels; in the 1920s popular works were sold in the cheap Shilling Series in England; the dust cover is a twentieth-century innovation; and during the Great Depression of the 1930s publishers brought out cheap paperback editions to sustain buying.

concepts.label: Manuscripts Before the Age of Print
concepts.cardText: India had a very rich and old tradition of handwritten manuscripts in Sanskrit, Arabic, Persian and various vernacular languages, copied on palm leaves or handmade paper and sometimes beautifully illustrated, pressed between wooden covers or sewn together. Manuscripts continued to be produced down to the late nineteenth century, well after print was introduced. However, they were highly expensive and fragile, had to be handled carefully, and could not be read easily as the script was written in different styles, so they were not widely used in everyday life. Even though pre-colonial Bengal had an extensive network of village primary schools, students very often did not read texts; they only learnt to write as teachers dictated portions of texts from memory, so many became literate without ever actually reading any kinds of texts.

concepts.label: Print Comes to India
concepts.cardText: The printing press first came to Goa with Portuguese missionaries in the mid-sixteenth century. Jesuit priests learnt Konkani and printed several tracts; by 1674 about 50 books had been printed in Konkani and Kanara. Catholic priests printed the first Tamil book in 1579 at Cochin and the first Malayalam book in 1713, and by 1710 Dutch Protestant missionaries had printed 32 Tamil texts. The English language press did not grow till quite late even though the East India Company began to import presses from the late seventeenth century. From 1780 James Augustus Hickey edited the Bengal Gazette, a weekly that described itself as a commercial paper open to all but influenced by none. He published advertisements and gossip about the Company's senior officials, which enraged Governor-General Warren Hastings, who persecuted Hickey and encouraged officially sanctioned newspapers to counter information that damaged the colonial government's image. By the close of the eighteenth century a number of newspapers and journals appeared, and Indians began to publish newspapers; the first was a weekly Bengal Gazette by Gangadhar Bhattacharya, who was close to Rammohun Roy.

concepts.label: Religious Reform and Public Debates
concepts.cardText: From the early nineteenth century there were intense debates around religious issues, carried out in public and in print. Printed tracts and newspapers spread new ideas and shaped the debate, and a wider public could participate. In Bengal controversies between social and religious reformers and the Hindu orthodoxy over widow immolation, monotheism, Brahmanical priesthood and idolatry produced tracts and newspapers printed in the everyday, spoken language. Rammohun Roy published the Sambad Kaumudi from 1821 and the orthodoxy commissioned the Samachar Chandrika to oppose him; Persian newspapers and the Gujarati Bombay Samachar followed in 1822. In north India the ulama, anxious about the collapse of Muslim dynasties and fearing colonial rulers would encourage conversion and change Muslim personal laws, used cheap lithographic presses, published Persian and Urdu translations of scriptures and printed religious newspapers and tracts; the Deoband Seminary, founded in 1867, published thousands of fatwas. Among Hindus too print encouraged reading religious texts in the vernacular, such as the Ramcharitmanas, and from the 1880s the Naval Kishore Press and Shri Venkateshwar Press published numerous vernacular religious texts, which could be read by the faithful anywhere or read out to illiterate groups. Print stimulated conflicting opinions but also connected communities in different parts of India, creating pan-Indian identities.

concepts.label: New Forms of Publication
concepts.cardText: Printing created an appetite for new kinds of writing. As more people could read, they wanted to see their own lives, experiences, emotions and relationships reflected in what they read. The novel, a literary form developed in Europe, ideally catered to this need and soon acquired distinctively Indian forms and styles; it opened up new worlds of experience and gave a vivid sense of the diversity of human lives. Lyrics, short stories and essays on social and political matters also entered the world of reading. By the end of the nineteenth century a new visual culture was taking shape: with more presses, visual images could be easily reproduced in multiple copies, painters like Raja Ravi Varma produced images for mass circulation, and cheap prints and calendars could be bought even by the poor to decorate their walls, shaping popular ideas about modernity and tradition, religion and politics, and society and culture. By the 1870s caricatures and cartoons in journals and newspapers commented on social and political issues, some ridiculing educated Indians' fascination with Western tastes and others expressing fear of social change, and there were imperial caricatures lampooning nationalists as well as nationalist cartoons criticising imperial rule.

concepts.label: Women and Print
concepts.cardText: Women's lives and feelings began to be written in vivid ways, and women's reading increased enormously in middle-class homes. Liberal husbands and fathers educated their womenfolk at home and sent them to schools set up in cities and towns after the mid-nineteenth century, and journals carried writings by women and explained why women should be educated. But not all families were liberal: conservative Hindus believed a literate girl would be widowed, and Muslims feared educated women would be corrupted by Urdu romances. Rebel women defied prohibitions: Rashsundari Debi learnt to read secretly in her kitchen and wrote Amar Jiban (1876), the first full-length autobiography in Bengali. From the 1860s Bengali women like Kailashbashini Debi wrote about women's experiences, and in the 1880s Tarabai Shinde and Pandita Ramabai wrote with passionate anger about the lives of upper-caste Hindu women, especially widows. In the early twentieth century journals written for and sometimes edited by women became popular, discussing women's education, widowhood, widow remarriage and the national movement. In Punjab, Ram Chaddha's Istri Dharm Vichar and the Khalsa Tract Society's booklets taught women to be obedient wives, and in Calcutta the Battala printed cheap popular books taken by pedlars to homes.

concepts.label: Print and the Poor People
concepts.cardText: Very cheap small books were brought to markets in nineteenth-century Madras towns and sold at crossroads, allowing poor people travelling to markets to buy them. Public libraries were set up from the early twentieth century, expanding access to books; they were located mostly in cities and towns and sometimes prosperous villages, and for rich local patrons setting up a library was a way of acquiring prestige. From the late nineteenth century issues of caste discrimination began to be written about in printed tracts and essays: Jyotiba Phule wrote about the injustices of the caste system in Gulamgiri (1871), and in the twentieth century B.R. Ambedkar and E.V. Ramaswamy Naicker (Periyar) wrote powerfully on caste and were read all over India. Local protest movements and sects created popular journals and tracts criticising ancient scriptures and envisioning a new and just future. Factory workers were too overworked and lacked education to write much, but the Kanpur millworker Kashibaba published Chhote Aur Bade Ka Sawal in 1938 to show links between caste and class exploitation, and by the 1930s Bangalore cotton millworkers set up libraries to educate themselves, sponsored by social reformers who wanted to restrict excessive drinking, bring literacy and sometimes spread nationalism.

concepts.label: Print and Censorship
concepts.cardText: Before 1798 the East India Company was not too concerned with censorship, and its early measures to control printed matter were directed against Englishmen critical of Company misrule, since criticisms might be used by critics in England to attack its trade monopoly. By the 1820s the Calcutta Supreme Court passed regulations to control press freedom. In 1835, faced with petitions from editors, Governor-General Bentinck agreed to revise press laws and Thomas Macaulay formulated new rules restoring the earlier freedoms. After the revolt of 1857 attitudes changed: enraged Englishmen demanded a clamp down on the native press, and as vernacular newspapers became assertively nationalist the government debated stringent control. The Vernacular Press Act of 1878, modelled on the Irish Press Laws, gave the government extensive rights to censor reports and editorials in the vernacular press; a newspaper judged seditious was warned and, if the warning was ignored, the press could be seized and its machinery confiscated. Despite repression, nationalist newspapers grew, reported colonial misrule and encouraged nationalist activities, and attempts to throttle criticism provoked militant protest and a cycle of persecution and protest: when Tilak wrote with sympathy in the Kesari about deported Punjab revolutionaries in 1907, he was imprisoned in 1908, provoking widespread protests. In the First World War 22 newspapers had to furnish securities under the Defence of India Rules, 18 of which shut down, and in August 1942 about 90 newspapers were suppressed. Gandhi said in 1922 that the fight for Swaraj and Khilafat was a fight for liberty of speech, liberty of the press and freedom of association.
